record.paper_title: Toward epidemic thresholds on temporal networks: a review and open questions
record.context_brief: Statistical network models and community detection
record.original_question: Most epidemic-threshold work on temporal networks assumes that the network is deterministic and fully observed, but many practical settings require uncertainty quantification, prediction of future interactions, and inference of latent community structure. How can results on epidemic thresholds for temporal networks be connected to statistical network models and community-detection methods so that threshold analysis remains usable when the network is only partially known or must be modeled probabilistically?

evidence.quote: Most of the existing literature on epidemic thresholds considers the network to be deterministic and fully observed. This approach does not allow for uncertainty quantification or future predictions of interactions.
Connecting the existing results on epidemic thresholds to statistical network models and community detection techniques can greatly broaden the applicability of these results.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a temporal network on a finite vertex set $V=\{1,\dots,n\}$, represented as a sequence of (possibly weighted) adjacency matrices $\{A_t\}_{t=1}^{T}$, where $A_t(i,j)$ encodes the strength or presence of an interaction between vertices $i$ and $j$ at discrete time $t$. On such a network run a Markovian SIS epidemic process: at each time step, an infected vertex $i$ infects a neighbor $j$ along edge $(i,j)$ at rate $\beta A_t(i,j)$, and each infected vertex recovers independently at rate $\delta>0$. The epidemic threshold $\tau^* = \tau^*(\{A_t\}, \delta)$ is the critical value of $\beta/\delta$ separating the regime where the expected time to extinction is $O(\log n)$ from the regime where it is $\exp(\Omega(n))$.

Now suppose the network is not deterministically observed but is generated from a statistical network model with latent community structure. Specifically, let $z:V\to\{1,\dots,K\}$ assign each vertex to one of $K$ communities, and let $\{A_t\}$ be drawn from a dynamic stochastic block model with community-pair interaction rates $B_t \in [0,1]^{K\times K}$, so that conditional on $z$ the entries $A_t(i,j)$ are independent Bernoulli$(B_t(z_i,z_j))$ random variables. Assume only a partial observation of $\{A_t\}$ is available (for instance edges revealed up to time $T_0<T$, or a subsample of edges).

Develop a framework producing:

(a) a definition of the epidemic threshold $\tau^*$ in this probabilistic, partially observed setting, together with a rigorous estimator $\hat\tau$ of $\tau^*$ computable from the observed portion of $\{A_t\}$ and from community labels inferred by a community-detection procedure;

(b) finite-sample concentration or consistency guarantees of the form $\hat\tau \to \tau^*$ (in probability, as $n\to\infty$ or $T\to\infty$) under stated identifiability conditions on the dynamic stochastic block model;

(c) valid uncertainty quantification (e.g.\ confidence intervals or posterior credible sets) for $\tau^*$ that incorporate both the randomness of the network model and errors arising from imperfect community recovery and from prediction of future interactions $\{A_t\}_{t>T_0}$.

The problem is to construct such a framework and to prove that it yields consistent estimation and asymptotically valid uncertainty quantification of the epidemic threshold under explicit, minimal assumptions on the dynamic stochastic block model.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction connecting epidemic-threshold analysis on temporal networks with statistical network modeling and community detection. No published work appears to provide a unified framework giving consistent estimation and uncertainty quantification of epidemic thresholds on partially observed temporal networks generated from dynamic stochastic block models, so the problem appears to remain open.
